issues.item: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Public Transport' is hard to justify from the rest of the profile. The triggers are auditory/name/voice reminders linked to childhood caregiver abuse, and the negative appraisals are shame/self-blame/meaninglessness. Avoiding public transport suggests a situational safety strategy tied to a specific external environment, but there are no threat, memory, or trigger items indicating transport-related danger, crowding, entrapment, or encounters with abuse reminders in that context. This makes the item clinically difficult to integrate with the rest of the selected profile and with the formulation, where maladaptive strategies are closely linked to triggers and appraisals.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Contamination/feeling dirty' is more characteristically tied to sexual trauma and is difficult to reconcile as a central appraisal in this profile of childhood physical abuse without any supporting memory, trigger, or threat content suggesting bodily violation themes.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: Avoiding evaluation of appearance/performance fits social-evaluative shame concerns, but the rest of the profile centers childhood caregiver abuse with auditory/name/voice reminders and self-blame/meaning loss. This strategy is not well supported by the listed triggers or appraisals and feels aimed at a different symptom cluster than the rest of the profile.

vignette:
# Amara

Amara was forty-seven when she first came to the clinic, though the exhaustion in her eyes made her look older. She had been a plumber for eighteen years—a profession she'd chosen deliberately, she said, because the work was straightforward, because pipes either leaked or they didn't, because there was no ambiguity in the solving. What she did not say, at least not directly, was that the job had allowed her to move through the world largely unsupervised, on her own schedule, answerable to no one but her clients and herself. That autonomy had felt like survival.

The trauma that shaped her began when she was five years old. Her uncle, the man her mother had asked to watch her while she worked, used to take her into the basement of his house in Lagos. He was a man with a particular voice—thin, reedy, with a habit of hissing his words through his teeth when he was angry. He would call her name in that voice, drawing it out in a way that made her stomach drop before he ever touched her. The physical abuse was severe and prolonged; what stayed with her most vividly was not the pain itself but the sound of his voice preceding it, the way he would call her name as if summoning her to something inevitable.

Amara's parents had brought her to America when she was eight, away from him, but the damage was already woven into her nervous system. For decades she had functioned reasonably well—she had married a kind man, built a career, maintained friendships. But in the past year, something had shifted. It had started with a sound. One of her clients, a woman in a professional office building, had a receptionist with a voice that was similar to her uncle's—not identical, but similar enough: that same thin quality, the same slight hiss. Amara had heard it through the office door as she was leaving a job, and her body had locked. She'd sat in her truck in the parking garage for twenty minutes, hands shaking, unable to drive.

After that, the world had begun to narrow. She started hearing her uncle's voice everywhere—in a cashier at the hardware store, in a neighbor's son visiting next door, in the voice of a police officer who had stopped her for a broken taillight. Each time, the old feeling returned: the sense that something terrible was about to happen, that she was about to be hurt. Worse, she had begun to believe that the reason these sounds triggered her so powerfully was something fundamental about who she was. She was broken. She was damaged in a way that made her incapable of functioning like a normal person. There was something defective in her that made her vulnerable to hurt, that made her unable to move past what had happened to her. The triggering sounds seemed to confirm this belief—they proved that she was weak, that she was the kind of person to whom bad things happened because of something intrinsic to her character.

To manage the mounting fear, Amara had begun avoiding anything that might expose her to these sounds. She started turning down jobs in office buildings and professional spaces. She stopped going to the grocery store at certain times, avoiding the cashiers whose voices unsettled her. She refused to go to the police station when she needed to renew her license, asking her husband to do it instead. Her avoidance also extended to people in uniforms or positions of authority—she would cross the street to avoid police officers, she would not attend community meetings where officials might speak. And when she was alone with her thoughts, she found herself dwelling on what her uncle had done, replaying the scenarios, imagining what he might have done had the circumstances been slightly different. She ruminated endlessly on his actions, on his cruelty, on the fact that he had never faced any real consequence for what he had done to her.

The rumination and the avoidance had begun to feed something darker. The more she avoided situations and people, the more her world shrank, the more she felt like a prisoner in her own life. And the more her world shrank, the more convinced she became that there truly was something fundamentally wrong with her—that a healthy person would not be so afraid, would not need to hide so much. Nothing in her life felt meaningful anymore. Her work, which had once been a source of quiet pride, now felt like a series of jobs she was canceling or avoiding. Her marriage, which had been genuinely warm, had grown distant; her husband could not understand why she would not leave the house some days, why she had become so rigid about where she would and would not go. The avoidance fed the negative thoughts, and the negative thoughts made the triggers feel even more dangerous. When she heard a voice that resembled her uncle's, she was certain it meant something was wrong with her for being so afraid. And because she believed something was fundamentally wrong with her, she could not imagine that exposure to these sounds might ever feel manageable.

It was her husband who finally insisted she seek help. He had noticed her pulling away, the way she flinched at certain sounds, the way she had begun to decline invitations and isolate herself. What frightened Amara most was not the prospect of therapy itself, but the possibility that a therapist might confirm what she already believed—that she was too broken to be helped, that the damage her uncle had done was permanent and defining. What she hoped for, though she barely dared to speak it aloud, was that somehow she might reclaim her life, that the sounds that now controlled her might lose their power, that she might become the kind of person who could simply hear a voice and move forward without her entire body betraying her.
